title: Empirical Evaluation of a Validator‑Assisted LLM NetOps Pipeline: A Paired Study with gpt-5‑mini on 400 Intent→Configuration Tasks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑002) to measure operational failure rates of LLM‑generated network configuration changes and the effect of a lightweight automated validator+single‑repair step. Using gpt‑5‑mini and a hosted NetOps adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1), we executed 400 unique intent tasks paired under two conditions: Direct‑apply (baseline) and Guarded (validator + at most one deterministic repair call). All tasks were executed in sandboxed emulator replicas with public/synthetic intents and public topology examples. Confirmatory analysis found zero operational failures in both conditions (Npairs=400; n11=400, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The paired difference (Guarded − Baseline) = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI 0.00–0.00, bootstrap resamples=10000, seed=1729); McNemar two‑sided p=1.0. The preregistered hypotheses that baseline failure ≥20% and that the validator would reduce failure by ≥40% were not supported. We report the full preregistration, execution manifest, scoring artifacts, and deterministic reconciliation. We discuss operational interpretations, plausible causes for the null effect (task scope, simulator/validator coverage, and model behavior), and threats to validity. All artifacts and analysis scripts are archived as referenced in the execution manifest.

sections.introduction: Motivation — LLMs are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration, remediation, intent translation). Prior work argues that model outputs must be bounded by validators, repair loops, or human approval to achieve operational reliability [W4415071524; doi:10.1002/nem.2313; W7161354925]. We preregistered a focused empirical study to measure (i) realistic failure rates when applying LLM‑generated configuration changes in sandboxed heterogeneous networks and (ii) the efficacy of a lightweight automated validator that may trigger a single deterministic LLM repair call (CAND‑2026‑002). Research question — In reproducible paired execution across 400 intents, does a validator+single‑repair reduce operational failures relative to direct application, and what are the operational failure characteristics? Contributions — (1) a machine‑readable preregistration (CAND‑2026‑002) and fully archived execution manifest; (2) a paired empirical run with gpt‑5‑mini and a hosted NetOps adapter over 400 unique intents; (3) deterministic confirmatory analysis showing no observed failures in either condition and an honest discussion of implications and limitations.
sections.related_work: LLM→NetOps translation, intent‑driven configuration, and generate–validate–repair architectures are active areas. Representative prior work includes intent‑driven translation and production frameworks [doi:10.1002/nem.2313; W4415071524; W7161354925], verifier‑guided IaC repair and TerraFormer (IaC) which emphasizes verifier feedback in closed loops (TerraFormer, W7124141852), and broad RAG/validator surveys motivating retrieval/validator use for factuality and safety [W4401857375]. Our study follows the practical, narrowly scoped experimental style advocated by recent AIOps/NetOps evaluations rather than producing a model leaderboard: we measure operational outcomes in a paired design with preregistered estimands.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design — We preregistered study CAND‑2026‑002 before execution. Key design elements: adapter_family=hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model=gpt‑5‑mini; two conditions (Baseline=Direct‑apply, Guarded=validator + ≤1 deterministic repair); paired within‑intent design; task_count=400 unique intents; completed_episode_count=800; planned/used model_calls≤800 (model_calls_used=400). Inputs — 400 intent items assembled from public/synthetic sources; three sandbox topology replicas derived from public topology examples; no private production traces. Transformation pipelines — direct_configuration_generation_v1 and generate_validate_repair_v1 (validator was deterministic; repair limited to one LLM call per task when validator failed). Execution logging and artifact preservation — preserved prompts, model outputs, adapter logs, scoring JSON artifacts, and hashes (see execution_manifest and artifact list). Primary estimand — paired difference in operational failure proportion: P(failure|Direct‑apply) − P(failure|Guarded). Analysis plan — preregistered paired analysis (bootstrap 95% CI, McNemar exact two‑sided test), BH FDR for secondary subgroup tests; complete_pair_primary failed‑call handling; seeds and bootstrap resamples fixed (seed=1729, 10000 resamples). Reproducibility — all raw outputs, scoring artifacts, and analysis scripts archived with SHA‑256 hashes in the execution_manifest.

Confirmatory outcome — every paired intent produced operationally successful application under both conditions (n11=400, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Primary analysis (preregistered): paired difference (Guarded − Baseline)=0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10000 resamples, seed=1729); McNemar two‑sided p=1.0. Result implications relative to preregistered hypotheses: H1 (baseline failure ≥20%) not supported; H2 (≥40% relative reduction) not supported — no failures observed to reduce. Secondary endpoints — outage‑duration distribution, rollback rates, vendor/change‑type subgroup breakdowns were uninformative because there were no recorded failures or rollbacks in the scoring artifacts; subgroup tables and per‑task scoring JSONs are archived. Deterministic reconciliation — all internal consistency checks passed; provider_call_audit shows 400 hosted model calls, 0 failed calls, 0 cache hits (see execution_manifest).
sections.discussion: Interpretation — In this constrained experimental setting (public/synthetic intents, emulator sandboxes, the hosted adapter, and gpt‑5‑mini), LLM outputs produced no observable operational failures under either direct application or guarded application. This outcome can plausibly arise for multiple non‑exclusive reasons: (a) the sampled intents were modest in scope and matched the model's training/distribution; (b) the sandbox topologies and validator coverage favored detectability and benign application; (c) modern LLMs (gpt‑5‑mini here) may have sufficient parametric and prompt‑driven knowledge for the chosen intent types; or (d) preprocessing and adapter scaffolding reduced risky outputs. Importantly, the null effect does not imply universal production safety. Operational implications — For low‑risk or narrowly scoped intent classes, a validator may have limited incremental benefit; however, absence of failures here should not be interpreted as general safety for broader, higher‑impact changes. The archive provides a reproducible baseline for future adversarial, higher‑stress, or production‑proximate experiments. Threats to validity (summary) — internal: single model and single adapter, possible prompt sensitivity; construct: simulator and validator may not represent production risks; external: sample of intents, topologies, and lack of vendor diversity reduces generality. Detailed limitations appear below. Exploratory follow‑ups — evaluate adversarial prompts, wider intent complexity, multi‑model comparison, and higher‑fidelity emulation (including staged canary and rollback mechanics).
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered paired NetOps experiment (400 intents, gpt‑5‑mini) comparing Direct‑apply and a lightweight validator+single‑repair pipeline. Under the constrained, sandboxed setting, we observed zero operational failures in both conditions; the validator produced no measurable reduction relative to baseline. This null result is scientifically informative: it documents a reproducible boundary case where current LLMs can complete modest intent→configuration tasks without recorded operational harm in emulated environments. However, the result does not generalize to complex, adversarial, or production settings. We release all artifacts, scoring outputs, and analysis scripts to support rigorous subsequent research that probes broader task difficulty, adversarial inputs, multi‑model heterogeneity, and higher‑fidelity validators. Reproducible artifacts are archived per the execution_manifest hashes and the preregistration (CAND‑2026‑002).

limitations: Single‑model study: only gpt‑5‑mini was tested — results do not generalize across models or model families.
Synthetic/public sandbox tasks: intents and topologies were public/synthetic and may underrepresent production complexity and adversarial inputs.
Simulator and validator coverage: emulator fidelity and the validator implementation may not capture real device idiosyncrasies, transient control‑plane dynamics, or vendor CLI peculiarities.
Zero‑failure ceiling effect: observed n_failures=0 prevents quantitative inference about validator efficacy for harder tasks; absence of observed failures constrains generalization.
Prompt and adapter sensitivity: potential sensitivity to prompt wording, adapter configuration, or hidden preprocessing that were not exhaustively varied.
Operational realism: no live production devices, staged canaries, or human operator interventions were included; external validity for production deployments is limited.
